subject: research/mimic-batch
professional: a researcher in authorship attribution / machine-generated-text detection (and applied statistics) reviewing for a workshop or TMLR-style venue; first checks: is the headline false-positive claim an expectation or one realisation of a single split, are batches independent, is the calibration leak-free

evidence.correctness: Ran `python3 batch.py` (91 s): results.json and results.txt regenerated byte-identical (git diff empty), so the table reproduces. Recomputed from results.json by my own script (/tmp/claude-0/ind.py): mean AUROC all-machine k=1/4/8/32 = 0.935/0.997/1.000/1.000, mean FPR k=1/4/8/32 = 0.074/0.075/0.087/0.150, p=0.5 k=8 AUROC 0.982, p=0.25 k=32 0.985, p=0.1 k=32 0.822: all match the README table. Independent check of the model scores with sklearn roc_auc_score on the full family (not batch.py's AUROC): recipes 0.867 (README quotes 0.88, which is the 150-human test-half value, so not wrong but not the same quantity); books 0.993 (README 0.99). Independent re-simulation of the headline FPR with my own code, a different seed and 20 random cal/test splits per family: recipes k=1 0.058 (sd 0.031), k=32 0.058 (sd 0.076); books k=1 0.042 (sd 0.029), k=32 0.112 (sd 0.098). README's books k=1 0.165 and k=32 0.596 are one split's realisation, not typical (my mean 0.042 and 0.112). Arithmetic is right; the split-level interpretation is the weakness (see claims).
evidence.completeness: Checked every README claim against files: batch.py, figure.py, results.json, results.txt, experiments/figure.svg exist; `pytest tests` gives '7 passed' as README says (7); per-family rows in results.txt match the README description; reads ../mimic-contexts/data/suite.jsonl.gz and ../mimic-threshold/threshold.py, both present and imported OK; ~2 min runtime claim true (91 s). The 'Next steps' (SPRT, max statistic, correlated batches, adapted imitators) are explicitly not done and flagged as such. No stubs or TODOs found. Live page not loaded by me (network not probed), so not scored on it.
evidence.verification: `python3 -m pytest tests` -> 7 passed in 0.76 s. Tests use synthetic Gaussians and cover auroc, 1/sqrt(k) spread, round(p*k)=0 skip, mixed-batch mean, FPR near 5%, dilution ordering. Seeded mutation 1: threshold quantile 1-target -> 1-2*target; test_fpr_near_target_and_tpr_grows_with_k failed (caught). Seeded mutation 2: test half set equal to the calibration half (`test = sh[idx[:n//2]]`), i.e. calibration leakage that defeats the project's central finding; 7 passed, NOT caught. No test exercises main() or the real-data path, no test pins results.json, no test on the independence between cal and test halves. Both mutations reverted with git checkout; git status clean.
evidence.craft: Read batch.py (88 lines), tests/test_batch.py, figure.py. Compact, vectorised (batch_means via fancy indexing), seeded, docstrings state the design, no copied engines (imports threshold.py). Defects: sys.path hack to import a sibling project; main() has no guard for a missing dataset; json.dump(open(...)) leaves file handles unclosed; one rng stream shared across k so results at a k depend on the earlier ks (reordering KS changes numbers); mixed batches always put the machine texts first (order irrelevant for a mean, harmless); one split per family with no repeat option, which is exactly what limits the science. No dead code.
evidence.claims: Verified numbers (table) match results.json. Unsupported or overstated: (1) 'The threshold, not the score, is what breaks ... 15% on average at k=32, 60% for books' is stated as a mechanism and a magnitude, but it rests on ONE random half-split per family; my 20-split re-simulation gives books k=32 mean 0.112 (sd 0.098) and recipes unchanged 0.058, so the 60% is a tail draw and the 'average 15%' is a single realisation with unknown variance (the qualitative growth of FPR variance with k is real, the stated magnitudes are not estimates). (2) 'Per-text FPR at k=1 drifts (books 16.5%)' is the same single-split artefact; my mean is 0.042. (3) 'Dilution costs about a factor of the machine share' is read off a 4-point grid with no fit. (4) 'extends mimic-recalib ... needs about 80 calibration texts' cites another project and was not re-derived. Limitations section is honest about i.i.d. batches, one statistic, one detector, and AI assistance and 'Preliminary' are disclosed. Wald/Sadasivan citations are real but Sadasivan et al. is about detectability bounds, not batch size; the link is loose. No disclaimer issue for a research page.
evidence.fitness: A researcher could rebuild the simulation and reuse batch.simulate for any score pool, and the question (how fast does a weak detector aggregate; how does a fixed-rule false-accusation rate scale with batch size) is practically relevant to moderators. Nearest prior work: pooling evidence is textbook (Wald 1945 SPRT; the Neyman-Pearson / CLT for means), and in the detector literature aggregation over multiple documents and calibration under distribution shift are covered in work on RAID (Dugan et al. 2024) FPR-at-fixed-threshold evaluation, Sadasivan et al. on detection bounds as sample size grows, and authorship-verification practice of pooling per-document scores. The AUROC rising with k is essentially the CLT on i.i.d. draws and is expected and not new. The potentially new angle (calibration-set error does not shrink with k, so a batch verdict inflates FPR) is a known fact about plug-in thresholds for sample means, and here it is shown on one split, not quantified, so not yet a result a researcher can cite. Because batches are bootstrap draws from <=150 texts per half, and real account texts are correlated, effects at k=32 largely reflect resampling a small pool. Not sound enough to build on without repeated splits.
evidence.domain: A detection researcher would want: bootstrap or repeated cross-fitting of the calibration split with CIs (missing, one split per family, 8 rows as the only variance); a calibration set sized to k and a conformal / permutation threshold; a bootstrap draw without replacement or across disjoint texts (duplicates occur at k=32 from 150 texts); a sequential or max/top-k statistic for sparse mixtures (acknowledged as not tested; the mean is known to be near-optimal only for dense shifts, so the p=0.1 result is a property of the mean); reporting TPR at a fixed low FPR (1% or 0.1%) as RAID and the detection literature do, not only 5%; and an adapted-imitator condition, which the project's own tracks aim at. Uses a weak n-gram LR as the detector, no LLM detector, so the headline cannot be compared with deployed tools. Leave-one-family-out is a good domain choice. Departures mostly stated; the single-split design is the main one.

defects.what: Headline false-accusation magnitudes (15% mean, 60% books at k=32, 16.5% books at k=1) come from one random cal/test split per family; 20 random splits give books 0.112 (sd 0.098) at k=32 and 0.042 at k=1. The mechanism is presented as measured when it is a single realisation.
Tests do not catch calibration leakage: setting the test half equal to the calibration half leaves all 7 tests passing, although the project's central finding depends on the halves being disjoint.
Per-text figure 'recipes 0.88' is the 150-human test-half AUROC; the full-family value is 0.867 by sklearn.
Shared rng stream across k, unclosed json file handles, no real-data test of main().

verdict: A small, honest, reproducible simulation (results regenerate byte-identically, 7 tests pass, the table's aggregates recompute exactly) whose arithmetic is right but whose most interesting claim, that fixed-rule batch verdicts inflate false accusations as k grows, is demonstrated on a single calibration split per family; repeating the split 20 times shrinks the book-family numbers from 0.60 to a mean near 0.11 with large variance. The AUROC-versus-k curve is the CLT on bootstrap draws and not new; the calibration-error angle is potentially useful but known in principle and unquantified. Tests are synthetic and miss a seeded leakage bug. Preliminary label is fair; it does not meet the bar (verification 2, claims 2, domain 2). Smallest fix: loop the cal/test split (e.g. 200 splits per family), report the mean and an interval for FPR, add a disjointness test.
